keep: The twenty-year delay is a story historians told later. He was busy, mostly with barnacles, and when Wallace's essay forced his hand the Origin took him thirteen months.
lede: The famous story has him sitting on his theory for twenty years, afraid of what it would do to him. He told his friends about it, and spent eight of those years on barnacles.
copy: Charles Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle on 27 December 1831, after two false starts that month, and was back at Falmouth on 2 October 1836. Four years and nine months. He came home with specimens and notebooks, and a decade of publishing them, the zoology of the voyage and then its geology. He had natural selection by 1838, after reading Malthus. On the Origin of Species proposed that living things descend, with modification, from common ancestors, and that the engine of the branching is natural selection: heritable variation winnowed by the struggle to survive and reproduce.

The Origin came out in 1859. What happened in the gap became the centre of his modern legend. Adrian Desmond and James Moore's biography of 1991 summed it up later as a man who 'had buried evolution for twenty years, petrified for his respectability'. John van Wyhe went back to the letters in 2007 and found no clear evidence for it. Darwin's belief in evolution was not a secret; everyone he named as a possible editor of his 1844 sketch knew of it. He had planned to finish the Beagle books first, then a short spell on invertebrates from 1846. The invertebrates grew into the barnacle monograph, which ran until 1854. He was slow with everything. He saw what worms do to soil in 1837 and published the book in 1881.

Wallace's essay arrived in 1858 and forced the abstract out. Darwin spent, in van Wyhe's word, a gruelling thirteen months writing it. The legend has the first edition selling out to the public on publication day, Thursday 24 November 1859. Darwin did write to Huxley that day that Murray 'sold whole Edition of my Book on first day'. What sold was the trade sale two days earlier, to booksellers. Murray had printed 1,250 copies, and 1,192 of them were for sale.

bio.why: The first of two volumes; the second is The Power of Place (2002). It places the science inside Darwin's household, letters and Victorian world, and, as van Wyhe notes, largely downplays a delay after 1844. This house has read van Wyhe, Freeman and the letters, not Browne.

contested: The delay itself. Desmond and Moore made it the central theme of their Darwin (1991): a man frightened for his respectability, holding back a theory he knew would be despised. John van Wyhe's 'Mind the gap' (Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 2007) answers that their case for the social climate is plausible but that no clear evidence ties it to anything Darwin thought or did; the gap was work in hand, done in the order he had planned. Van Wyhe was not first. Cannon argued in 1976 that Darwin needed the twenty years to build his case. And van Wyhe concedes his own explanation, that age and reputation made it easier to publish in 1859, has no evidence behind it either. Darwin's 1876 line that he would not write even a sketch for fear of prejudice is the strongest text for the fear reading; Browne suggests the prejudice he meant was his own.
